title: Mood Atlas
description: Mood Atlas is an Obsidian plugin that expands your emotional vocabulary as you journal. Type any emotion word followed by a trigger key to pull up all the feeling words in the same emotional region - helping you find the most precise word for what you're experiencing. Type an emotion word, then press ^ (configurable). A dropdown appears showing all emotions in the same region, so you can choose the one that fits best. Three emotion word lists are available, and each can be customized in the plugin settings: Hoffman/NVC Combined (the default), the Hoffman Institute feelings list, and the feelings list from Marshall Rosenberg's Nonviolent Communication. Get Mood Atlas in the Obsidian community plugins · Source on GitHub

title: Paris Rooftops: Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois & the BHV
description: Climbing Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois
imageAlt: Silhouette standing on a chimney beside the church's bell tower

images.caption:
I studied abroad spring quarter of my junior year at Stanford during which I met up with several cataphiles through Couchsurfing. Together we crawled beneath the streets of Paris, crawling into manholes after lifting 200 pound plaques, following winding chatières of the 200 mile catacomb network, climbing into chantières and up échafaudage to rooftops. Les plaques (manhole covers), les chatières (narrow passages of the catacombs, literally cat-holes), les chantières (construction areas), l'échafaudage (scaffolding), les toits (roofs), les cataflics (police in the catacombs) -- I've learned French since middle school, but it's amusing to reflect on how much my now peculiar vocabulary set has been shaped by my experiences in Paris. 

The church L'église Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois and the 1st district city call, la mairie du 1er arrondissement de Paris, stand side by side right across from the world-famous Louvre. The church, founded in the 7th century and rebuilt many times over several centuries, was the church for the royalty of the Louvre palace. Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois was the very first building I ever climbed in Paris, May 2013. 

I met a lot of UE friends in Paris, but this first climb was done solo, on a complete whim...

images.caption: I had just popped out of a manhole like a dusty stray cat an hour ago at 2AM, after having spent a wonderful evening painting a small mural in an auxiliary network of the catacombs. The night lights were a beautiful gold that mixed purple with the soft blue skies. The air was so invitingly warm that instead of taking the Noctilien night bus I decided to walk home from Châtelet to the Champs-Élysées where I lived with my host family. As I walked briskly I happened to pass by this church that a Parisian Couchsurfer had informed me was climbable. I paused ... just long enough to convince myself this was a good idea, but not long enough to faze myself with all the possible risks. What was the primary risk? (Stupidity, actually.) I was alone and didn't want to lug my huge backpack full of paints and paintbrushes that I had used in the catacombs up to a rooftop. So, I casually tucked my pack with > $3000 worth of stuff (iPhone, laptop, DSLR, canera lens) in the streets below behind some scaffolding, but still very visible. From an outsider's perspective it probably looked like a homeless person's sack of stuff. Stupid, but I was lucky. I ended up climbing scaffolding until I reached the stone angel statue at the very top of the roof of la mairie. I stared across to the Louvre on the other side. It was surprisingly quiet for the City of Lights. Wide streets, no people, the Seine to the left, calm, only unidentifiable susurrus in the streets below. On the other side of the church I could see La Samaritaine, once the largest department store in Paris, since abandoned. Yet the lights were on on all floors, a waste of electricity and slightly eerie.
images.alt: Mairie du 1er facade and the bell tower from below

images.caption:
The second time I went rooftoping at this church I brought a friend, Maxime, who was the person who first introduced me to the illicit network of the Paris catacombs. We became good friends during that spring and shared many adventures -- a few misadventures -- together. We got up close and personal with the gargoyle statues protruding from the walls, and the intricate rose window. Up a staircase, we even found a window that opened into the body of the church itself. We stared down at the pews below, swallowed in darkness.

We maneuvered our way up walls and around buttresses, avoiding pigeon poop, pigeon feathers, and dead pigeons in nooks and crannies---it wasn't all glamorous!
images.alt: Paris rooftops and chimneys under a cloudy night sky

images.caption:
Satisfied with our exploration, we took a break and lay on the roof. Maxime and I stared at the cloudy sky and shared a conversation as Daft Punk's "Get Lucky" and Lou Reed's "Walk on the Wild Side" murmured from his music player. Magic wasn't Disneyland -- it was 70 ft underground in the catacombs and 50 ft above ground on the roofs of Paris. The world felt huge. 

This was my very first time engaging with UE outside of roof hacking my college campus and I suddenly felt very empowered to explore anything I wanted. Paris was freeing; I slept very little and life was brilliant.

images.caption: Roof of Bazar Hôtel de Ville The clock was ticking: these were my final hours in Paris before I flying back to SFO. I already had a picture of what the the perfect conclusion to my study abroad experience in Paris would be: a night or rooftopping, a last hurrah with strangers-become-close-friends. We climbed to the roof of Bazar Hôtel de Ville and stayed there until the sky began its transformation into a more gentle blue. It was 5AM. My flight from Paris back to California was in a few hours, yet I was on a roof top with Avrell, Maxime, and Éric. I was so reluctant to ride a vélib bike back home and say goodbye to everyone and to Paris. Maybe there was something in the back of my mind ... a fear of saying goodbye. Paris will stay, but buildings change, people change, expectations change. The next time I'm back, the context will change. I will change quite a bit, too.

images.caption: Rewinding the night a bit, it was 3AM and we climbed our way to the 7e story: the BHV dome. Inside we found a surprising collection of flags, BHV corporate actions, old newspapers, stamps, a typewriter, files of "dubious BHV customers" that made us chuckle. Maxime even found a tiny diver figurine, now dubbed "François." I brought him home to the US and he's currently in a folder with my passport and old plane tickets. Does this mean I value François as much as my passport? More importantly, can the poor guy breathe in that stuffy folder I'm trapping him in? (The answer is yes, because he's a diver...) Les bêtises: Averell and Éric busied themselves with a flag switch-a-roo. They wanted to lower the iconic BHV flag and replace it with a few that were more colorful. "Which flags should we choose?" They pondered over their choices, skipping over France and the USA. "Hm, let's choose Mexico because Mexico is a nice country." Then they chained together a few more flags for a greater effect. They gave me the old BHV flags to keep. "You know the funny thing is, now that you have both flags, they won't have a replacement anymore to put up." From the roof we could see le Tour Saint-Jacques, the beautiful Place de L'hôtel de Ville almost dead center of Paris, la tour Montparnasse (which you really can't not see if you're in Paris), le Centre Pompidou, la tour Eiffel, and the usual smattering of ornate churches. Another lovely view. When it came time I biked back home with Maxime -- whizzing past early construction workers, past a city that was waging war between two clashing colors of 5AM city-light-yellow and 5AM light-sky-blue, past the half-constructed annual ferris wheel in the Jardin des Tuileries -- to arrive home to pack my luggage completely, utterly à l'arrache ... (comme toujours.) From Somewhere Within the BHV More snapshots from within the "secret" dome of Bazar Hôtel de Ville where we found old flags, corporate actions and paper stocks, old newspapers, stamps, a typewriter, files of "dubious BHV customers," and more. The discovery of all these historical-cultural items came as a complete surprise to the four of us, who had originally climbed to the roof for the views, but it turns out Le Parisien had conveniently published article 8 years ago, which explained all of this "trésor caché" as they called it. Kudos to Averell for finding the article and emailing to me after I had returned to California.

title: Paris Catacombs (GRS)
description: "Je ne savais pas, je ne savais pas, je ne savais pas ... TOUT ÇA!!" A man's singing and an accordion emanated from Maxime's speakers and filled Salle Soleil (The Sun Room.) The music bounced off the limestone walls that were covered in paintings, reverberating down the small, pitch-black hole that we crawled through get here. I lay on a hammock, headlamp around my neck, wet boots concealing sopping socks, wet from the rainwater that floods certain passages of the catacomb network. It was 3AM, and my soaked socks added another dimension to the inherent chill of being so many stories underground Paris. In my hands I cupped a mug of warm, sugary tea that Maxime had brought in a thermos. Nearby was a stone table that a cataphile had carved years ago, now adorned with Maxime's candles, cherry tomatoes, a can of cheap corner store beer, and portable music speakers. There is an extensive map of the Grand Réseau Sud, the major catacomb network in Paris. The room names stirred imagination: Salle de Human Bomb. Petite Salle Rouge. Le Cellier. La Plage. Salle Soleil. To be written (notes for now): - Hours just sitting there chatting and listening to music. - Candles, candles, candles. A culture of candles. Apparently it's also popular for cataphiles to use carbide lamps as the miners once did in these very same networks. - A few more trips underground confirmed the tradition of wine, snacks, hammock, music, and candles - Things that surprised me: wetness, scuba diving, paintings, carvings, history, scavenger hunts (people leave "les tracts"), cataflics - There is art, but there is also destruction. - Plenty of people write about their experiences in the catacombs, from National Geographic articles to urbex blogs to youtube videos (link)

title: Yosemite
description: A collection of classic moderate rock climbs on the Eastern end of Yosemite National Park feat. Cathedral Peak and Eichorn Pinnacle; Tenaya Peak; Matthes Crest; Mt Conness. Yosemite was my gateway into high Sierra climbing. It was where I experienced so many firsts. Tenaya Peak was my first alpine trad climb. Cathedral Peak was the first time I made a new friend and climbing partner from a chance encounter on the descent. Matthes Crest was the first time death from climbing felt tangible when we saw a search and rescue helicopter fly terribly close and later learned that someone had fallen while on the same route as us earlier that day. Mt Conness was my first epic in the mountains. As the leader of the group, I didn’t have the mindspace to feel fear: I was solely focused on three things, staying safe, routefinding, and supporting my partner. I comforted my partner as the more experienced climber, even though I barely had much experience under my belt myself. It’s funny how you rise to the occasion. We pushed upwards through a black moonless night to summit at 2AM. We forced ourselves to make forward progress walking like zombies. We succumbed to shivering naps under rocks when our eyelids grew unbearably heavy. At sunrise we were filled with an indescribable mix of relief and elation. We waited until the golden rays of morning basked our numb bodies in warmth and lit the surrounding peaks aglow to reveal the path back home.

title: Death Valley
description:
Overshadowed by its more famous sibling Yosemite, Death Valley National Park receives less fanfare. With no expectations, I was blown away. There is no light pollution so the stars actually twinkle at night. I was so moved as a wee 13 year old that I wrote a poem about the night I saw the stars come alive.

I’ve returned many times since, always to show friends this special place in my heart.

title: All 汉字 Hànzì On Deck
description: Spaced Repetition Flashcards (And A Bad Pun). A spaced repetition Mandarin flashcard app. Cards and layout are driven by a Google Sheet, so updating the vocabulary needs no code changes. title: Career Mind Map
description: Inspired by the book Designing Your Life, mind maps are a tool for expanding possibilities before narrowing them down. Instead of asking "What job should I get?", start with themes and branch into related ideas, applying lateral thinking to find new connections and alternate life directions. Pick three starting points: an area of interest or an activity during which you were really engaged, something that really energizes you in your work and life, and an activity or experience where you get into a flow state. Career Mind Map branches each one out into related ideas and possible paths. Try Career Mind Map · Source on GitHub

title: The Eastern Sierra
description:
A few years ago I discovered a letter that resonates deeply with how I feel about being in the mountains. It was penned by legendary photographer Ansel Adams and later published in Letters of Note. In 1936, in the midst of an overwhelming workload and the near-demise of his marriage, Ansel Adams suffered a nervous breakdown. After a stay in the hospital, desperately in need of escape, Adams returned with his family to the one place where he could find solace: Yosemite, California.

As his health returned, he wrote this letter to his best friend, Cedric Wright. A violinist and wilderness photographer, Wright was Adams’s mentor and closest friend. In his autobiography, Adams described Wright as “almost an occupant of another world and a creator and messenger of beauty and mysteries. Perhaps his greatest gift was that of imparting confidence to those who were wavering on the edge of fear and indecision; often it was me.”

June 19, 1937

Dear Cedric,

A strange thing happened to me today. I saw a big thundercloud move down over Half Dome, and it was so big and clear and brilliant that it made me see many things that were drifting around inside of me; things that related to those who are loved and those who are real friends.

For the first time I know what love is; what friends are; and what art should be.

Love is a seeking for a way of life; the way that cannot be followed alone; the resonance of all spiritual and physical things. Children are not only of flesh and blood — children may be ideas, thoughts, emotions. The person of the one who is loved is a form composed of a myriad mirrors reflecting and illuminating the powers and thoughts and the emotions that are within you, and flashing another kind of light from within. No words or deeds may encompass it.

Friendship is another form of love — more passive perhaps, but full of the transmitting and acceptance of things like thunderclouds and grass and the clean granite of reality.

Art is both love and friendship, and understanding; the desire to give. It is not charity, which is the giving of Things, it is more than kindness which is the giving of self. It is both the taking and giving of beauty, the turning out to the light the inner folds of the awareness of the spirit. It is the recreation on another plane of the realities of the world; the tragic and wonderful realities of earth and men, and of all the inter-relations of these.

I wish the thundercloud had moved up over Tahoe and let loose on you; I could wish you nothing finer.

Ansel

images.caption: As a photographer I’ve always appreciated the beauty of the mountains. I wanted to get closer. I wanted to know a mountain by more than its triangle caricature. But how was I going to teach myself the skills to scale that granite when I didn’t have any climber friends?
images.alt: Sun rising behind jagged granite peaks

images.caption: In 2016 I moved to San Francisco. Riding a motivation wave from a relationship break-up and a renewal of energy as I started to overcome crippling imposter syndrome at my first software engineering job, I decided I wanted to climb. Without friends to mentor me, I scoured google and joined Sierra Mountaineering Club (SMC) where I built a solid foundation in mountaineering and rock climbing.
images.alt: Mountaineer in a yellow jacket climbing a snowy couloir

images.caption: From that year onward many summer weekends have been spent in the Eastern Sierra. I buckle up for 8 hour one-way sleep-deprived drives to and from the mountains. The mountains test my mental strength and patience. The mountains fill me with awe and a sense of smallness that help me let go of the unimportant things in life. Some  say the mountains are their church.

title: Dark Divide 300
description:
You’ve probably heard the saying: “If you think you are enlightened, go spend a week with your family.” I have my own version now: If you think you are enlightened, go spend five hours on Juniper Ridge.

Juniper Ridge is the infamous crux of the Dark Divide 300, a self-supported bikepacking race through the southern Washington Cascades, covering 340 miles and 33,230 feet of elevation gain. The route’s namesake is the Dark Divide Roadless Area within Gifford Pinchot National Forest, which organizer and route creator Ben Everett describes as “one of the most rugged and beautiful landscapes on the continent.” At its heart lies Juniper Ridge, where Ben warns “racers will push their bikes more than ride them for the next 10 or so miles.” Juniper Ridge falls almost exactly at the route’s halfway point, giving the course a kind of structural elegance: the midpoint is also the high point is also the crux.

Portrait of me at the starting line (last photo) by Kae-Lin Wang

title: The Japanese Odyssey
description:
[35mm film photos taken on 6 disposable cameras over thirteen and a half days]

Two thousand three hundred kilometers long, maybe more. Forty-six thousand meters of ascent. Guaranteed. Three hundred twenty-four hours to complete. The Japanese Odyssey leads with numbers front and center on its website. The next line feels like a dare: “Be prepared for the most scenic yet punishing ride you’ll ever attempt.”

On October 3, 2025, 84 cyclists from 24 countries departed from the base of Sakurajima volcano in southern Japan. There was no fixed route and no support. Over the next thirteen and a half days, each rider would chart their own path north to Matsumoto, linking 20 mandatory checkpoints across the country’s most remote and mountainous terrain.

The theme of the 2025 Japanese Odyssey was “The Forgotten Tōge.” The forgotten mountain pass. There is a dreamlike quality to the official route description:

“Your adventure begins at the foot of Sakurajima volcano, nestled in Kagoshima Bay. Soon, you’ll leave the main roads behind and venture into the lush, humid forests of Kyushu. Next, board a ferry to Shikoku and explore the island’s most secluded forest roads. From there, journey through Nara and Mie prefectures, where you’ll have the chance to experience the breathtaking autumn colors these regions are famous for. Take a quick ferry to Ise, then continue northward, culminating your journey deep in the heart of the Japanese Alps.”

It is a romantic paragraph. It does not mention crying on a bidet at three in the morning. Or the chewed-up tires and dented rims. The unrelenting rain. The roads torn open by typhoons. The fetal-position naps on the side of the road.

Bikepacking ultra events promise suffering. Japan softens the edges just a little. Konbini are open around the clock, which means a rider can roll into a convenience store at 2 a.m., soaked to the bone, and be revived by a hot meal, hot coffee, and a fresh pair of Family Mart-branded socks. Local sentō offer a chance to rinse off that second skin of salt and dirt. Internet cafes offer a place to sleep by the hour. Vending machines appear on the loneliest of roads. But when the clock doesn’t stop, relief is only temporary...

https://bikepacking.com/plog/japanese-odyssey-voice-memos/

title: Panoche Hills
description:
We spent our first night around a campfire at Mercey Hot Springs, listening to Isaac describe the Panoche Hills. The Panoche Hills are a desert ecosystem located an hour west of Fresno, California. The hills are an oxymoron, seemingly barren and lush at the same time. Doubletrack dirt roads wind in and out of windswept grasses. Rippling hills that pan out as far as the eyes can see. “The real kicker is the second climb. Very steep. Very loose.” Isaac muses, as his wok hisses over the campfire. “And when the sand gets wet it’s the stickiest clay in the world. Wheels go to from free spinning to not turning in 2 rotations and wrecks bearings.” Luckily tomorrow’s forecast was clear. I threw on my 47mm WTB Ventures, topped them off with sealant, and replaced both brake pads before this weekend trip. I attached extra bottle cages to the fork of my Thesis, too. There’s no cell reception; “bring everything you might need” was our mantra …
To read more, check out the story in print form in Dropped Magazine Vol. 3 https://www.droppedmag.com/shop/p/issue-02-n79ym GPX route on Strava: https://www.strava.com/activities/5105675109

title: Agra + Jaipur
description:
In November 2019 I spent a week in Gurgaon, India on a business trip. I was itching to cover more ground so I booked day tours to Agra and Jaipur.

“Have you heard about the truck culture in India?” my guide Karni Singh asks. Indian truck drivers adorn the backs of their trucks with colorful cloths that flap wildly down the motorways. “They also write quotes, witty jokes, philosophical things. They also just write names of family and friends. And almost always the names of their exes.” I laugh. Even though I can’t make sense of the Hindi painted onto the sides and backs of each truck, I see that each has a distinct personality. It feels like an externalized, motorized version of the driver inside.

My guide for my Jaipur Pink City tour has a masters in French literature. How many people in his school studied this subject? One. His passion project is translating French plays into Hindi. When he speaks, a “donc” slips out every few sentences. It’s endearing.

I look out the window of the car. Teenage girls in braids and blue school uniforms. A man wearing a pink jumpsuit along a perfectly matching teal pastel backdrop. Loose bricks and piles of rubble are shoveled into molehills; it looks like the sidewalk is tearing itself apart. Three men pedal their bikes each pulling cart of flowers. Stray dogs. The morning sun is a red-orange hazy orb. One fat brown cow.

Karni tells me about the caste system that has since been abolished, but is still an undercurrent. The men of the Singh caste can be identified by their earrings, he says. I can see his.

I see two boys coding hands as they ride their bikes through a side street. We make eye contact and they giggle sweetly before looking away, abashed.

We turn onto the highway, peppered with signs in big bold letters that warn the unruly to “Maintain lane discipline” and that “Over speeding will invite prosecution.” Two kids sip drinks on the back of dad’s motorcycle.

We pass through Shahjahanpur, dubbed “Japan of India” because so many Japanese factories are there.

I spy a flock of rowdy monkeys on the side of the freeway and we pull over. Two shopkeepers were selling watermelons from their carts. The monkeys go nuts. It is hard to tell if this is an intentional tourist “trap” to entertain foreign visitors, or just serendipity.

Jaipur is the capital and the largest city of the Indian state of Rajasthan. Rajasthan is a desert region in the west. Karni tells me that North India is more mixed with immigrants from Arabic countries or Iran. South India is more “Indian” and more conservative, he says.

At the palace, the home of Jaipur royal family, I was surprised to see hurried workers stringing up colorful pink and yellow flowers and cloths, sequins and lights around the palace inner courtyards. A wedding was happening tonight. The royal family may host wedding receptions for their close family friends.

I was lucky to be at the right place at the right time.

title: Old Delhi
description:
Men crouch by their storefronts, pouring basins of cold water over their leathery skin. As a part of their morning ritual the shopkeepers of Old Delhi bathe their bodies out in the open. The typically hectic Chandni Chowk market is quiet at 6am. But tucked in a winding alley while the rest of the world yawns awake, a scant team of five workers toil away. They are kulcha bread makers who bake and distribute 40 thousand kulcha breads every day.

Here I am in the heart of it all, to witness the intimate ritual of Old Delhi waking up.

These kulcha makers move like clockwork. Each man has one job: one man manages the oven. One man takes the baked kulcha tray and slides it across the ground to the next man. This man constructs neat stacks 24 trays high. Another man has the job of moving these stacks back and forth. This routine outputs 4 breads every 3 seconds!

This is impressive manpower, but Anchit reminds me there are kulcha machines that do this work far more efficiently. In this case though, technology is purposefully set aside for the sake of creating more jobs.

Next, we bike through Khari Baoli, Asia's largest spice market. Anchit points out a women shopkeeper, calm and poised. She’s the only woman shopkeeper in this market and she took on this work as the head of the household when the patriarch of the family died. We make an unexpected turn into a building and spiral up an outdoor staircase where spice workers labored away on each level. Anchit equates this to modern day slavery; they work for 10 months at a time toiling and living in these quarters without seeing their family. During the other 2 months they return home, but only to provide the manpower to swap out the farm crops.

Our final destination is the Sikh temple of the old city, Gurudwara Sis Ganj Sahib ji. We take off our shoes and glide through a shallow pool of water to clean our feet. We also tie pink cloths to cover our hair before stepping inside the place of worship. Unexpectedly, I find a community kitchen beyond the prayer halls. It’s all hands on deck: women are sitting crossed legged on the ground rolling kulcha dough into balls. A portly man oversees a massive boiling pot of lentils, the lip of the pot rising from his feet up to his waist. Outside under an awning, women and men sit together and chop vegetables. These are men and women are all volunteers, donating their time to the community before they start their work day. The Sikh religion focuses on doing good. I learn that every man and woman must donate 10% of their income or 10% of their time volunteering.

We visit the mess hall where men and women sit in neat rows, eating from their trays, drinking chai. A young boy walks around scooping lentils onto their plates. A man smiles at me and insists I take a bag of mystery crackers. This is why no one in Old Delhi ever dies of starvation, Anchit proclaims proudly. Anyone can visit the temple for a meal, even if they are not Sikh. Free housing is provided, too. No questions asked.

That was the final leg of an eye-opening day. But let’s rewind—how did I get here? For my last day of my business trip in India I booked a city bike tour with SpinMonkey Tours. It started at 6am. I was staying in the city of Gurgaon which meant I needed to get up at  4am to take a long taxi ride. When I was dropped off the sun had not yet risen. All the shops on the block were closed. Wild dogs roamed the unkempt street. I had no idea if I was where I should be. Many adventure starts with slight discomfort and nervous anticipation, after all. The discomfort was quickly forgotten after I was greeted by Anchit, the founder of the bike tour company.  As we wove through the overwhelming traffic of Old Delhi via bike, dodging rickshaws, pedestrians, horse wheeled carts, mopeds, and the occasional water buffalo, he showed me the city through his eyes.

title: Chamonix
description: Europeans sure know how to climb in style. I’m accustomed to weekends in the Eastern Sierra that look like this: wrap up work on a Friday afternoon and drive 7 hours into the night. Sleep in the car. Hike heavy packs to base camp on Saturday, kick off summit day Sunday with an alpine start as early at 3am, summit, decamp, and drive 7 hours back to the city. It's 1am by the time I get back home, leaving just a few hours to conk out before the Monday workday. Contrast my reality with this one: in July 2018 my climbing partner Derek and I made a trip to Chamonix. Every morning we would wake up at 6am, saunter a few blocks from our apartment to the gondola, play in the mountains, then catch the gondola back down just in time to wine and dine. Rinse and repeat. No matter how battered we were after a day out we knew we'd be coddled up in cozy blankets reading a book by sunset. Chamonix was a treasure trove. We grew accustomed to mixed climbing, building confidence in delicately toeing cracks in the rock with our steel crampons. Many of the easy and moderate routes were crowded, which—thankfully—I found more entertaining than frustrating. The summit of Petit Aiguille Verte was a jamboree of climbers, guided and unguided, from France, Germany, Italy, the USA, Japan. On Grand Montets we passed a Brit yelling to his partner, “Even though this terrain is easy you should still place pro. Don’t just wander up like a muffin!“ Climbers in bright jackets wove in and out of the snowy ridge like animated Christmas lights. It was only when the weather took a turn for the worse that we could experience this alpine playground in solitude. One such day was when we climbed the famous Arête des Cosmiques. The two of us found ourselves alone on this popular ridge. We traded crowds for snow, hail, and thunder. Mont Blanc cheekily hid behind the thick fog; we could only imagine the beautiful mountains that towered around us. A truly alpine experience! Iced eyelashes. Numb fingers jamming into hand cracks. Swearing. Bruised knees. Happy hearts. We were exalted as we clambered back onto the platform and caught the last gondola back to Chamonix. Photo featured in Strava Best of 2018 Photo Contest

title: Marrakech
description:
Isn’t it magical to see a city inverted? We arrived in Marrakech under looming rainclouds. Below the horizon of grey, the Medina is a swath of pink maze-like walls. It’s the inversion of what we’re used to: cities of grey high-rises against pink sunset skies.

Alice, Claudio, and I stayed in the Northeastern neighborhood of the Medina (old city) that had a rooftop patio that overlooked a tannery. The narrow stairwell leading 4 flights up to the rooftop smelled strongly of jasmine incense. It was only at the top could you smell the unpleasant but bearable scent of raw animal hide.

Despite the scent, we enjoyed spending time on the rooftop where we had a sweeping view of the entire city. Drying clothes, drying food, and broken furniture scatter the neighboring rooftops. The rooster crows at odd hours. Moped motors purr in the distance from every which way. And most strikingly, when the clock strikes three, chanting male voices sing through loudspeakers situated throughout the city—none of them in unison—a powerful hum echoing across the city in a call to prayer.

title: Zermatt
description:
Zermatt was the second stop of my solo trip after graduating from Stanford. By chance I was in town for the 150th anniversary of the first ascent of the Matterhorn.

To honor the infamous climb, local mountain guides installed solar lamps along the original route taken by Whymper and his ill-fated party. At night the lights would ceremoniously turn on one by one until the path reached the summit.

Illuminated, it looked like a constellation of stars had sighed, tired from sailing the skies, and had spread itself across the mountain to slumber.

title: Construction Crane Above Paris
description:
I was still meeting new friends (and still climbing things) even on my 2nd to last day in Paris. That night I was introduced to Cigale via a mutual Couchsurfing friend. Cigale was an Australian photographer who had been living in Paris for two years. He was quite the character; he sported a classy Salvador Dalí mustache, was an amazing storyteller, and had constructed a room in the west catacomb networks of the GRS. In fact "Cigale," his pseudonym, was an homage to his mustache. I asked Cigale if he wanted to join Averell, Jean-Christophe and I that night as we returned to a small and obscure network in which Averell and Jean-Christophe were constructing a room. I guess I could be considered the temporary "artist-in-residence" there ;-)

After a few hours of painting and storytelling underground, we exited the catacombs at 2am. Cigale and I biked north because he lived near the Bastille and I lived near the Champs-Élysées. As we crossed the Seine, we saw a towering construction crane along bank and decided to give it a climb. Neither of us had ever climbed a crane, but the excitement was mutual.
imageAlt: Climber standing on the crane jib above Paris under a full moon

images.alt: Climber standing on the crane jib above Paris under a full moon
Paris rooftops and the Seine from the top of the crane
Two climbers on the crane platform looking over the city
The Seine and its embankments lit up at night

images.caption: We hopped the fence and climbed up rung by rung, ascending the construction crane. Once at the top, we climbed to the jib of the crane and drank in the surreal 360 view of Paris lights and the beautiful Seine, shimmering under a full moon. Cigale drank some water, then poured a bit over the side of the crane. "Water for my homies!" he exclaimed. It was an incredulous situation that despite being my second to last night in Paris before flying back to the states, I found myself at the tip of a construction crane at 3AM with an Australian photographer-cataphile. Surreal. Damn, everything was surreal. "Do you recognize all the buildings?" Cigale asked me. I was excited to identify quite a few: the glowing green of the l'Institute de la Mode jumped out at me. Then Notre Dame and the Panthéon. l'Institut du Monde Arabe with its glowing green horizontal lines. In the distance I could even make out l'Arc du Triomphe, and impressively, la Defense behind it too. The clock of the Musée d'Orsay, maybe? "Nope! that's actually the Gare de Lyon", Cigale corrected me. I also recognized Parc de Bercy right across the river, Monmarte and Sacré Coeur in the distance, and too many ornate churches to count ... Absolutely breathtaking. Due to the full moon and light pollution it was a starless night, but down below our feet, the entire world glowed. As we climbed down I asked Cigale, "Do you think you'll stay in Paris for the rest of your life?" Usually when I ask people questions about the future I get understandably uncertain responses; I was surprised to hear him respond with a confident "Yup!" Hearing that somehow gave me a comforting warmth. He loved Paris. The view looking down:
images.alt: Climber at the crane railing above the Seine

images.caption: "Don't think I would've done this if I were by myself," Cigale told me after we climbed down and back over the construction fencing. He also admitted he was a bit acrophobic. I grinned. We turned around to face the fence one last time. To enter, Cigale had climbed over a weak part of the fence and had consequently created a huge bulge at the top. I was second to climb over, and instead, I spotted a better route via clinging onto some wood reinforcements on the side -- once again, the idea of taking time to puzzle out the best routes. "Well," he defended himself, "I wanted to spend the least time possible outside looking like a suspect just standing and looking like I wanted to climb over!" "Who knows," he added, "Maybe they'll think it was some drunk guy that fell."
images.alt: Looking straight down through the crane's red frame

title: Williamsburg Bridge
description: [July 2014] It promised to be a pretty remarkable day where there would be a double dose of natural phenomena: a supermoon and Manhattanhenge, a twice-a-year solar phenomenon is during which the setting sun is aligned with the east-west streets of the main street grid of Manhattan. And later, it turns out, this would also be the day we climbed up to the top of the Williamsburg bridge.
imageAlt: Williamsburg Bridge roadway lit up at night, seen from the tower

images.caption: When I meet someone I don't know or go somewhere I've never been my senses are subconsciously alert for signs: a sign that things are going to be good or terrible. Lucas called to tell me that he had just arrived at the subway station and put me on hold as he walked around to find me. As he strolled I could through the receiver that he was casually whistling a tune. I knew this was going to be good. Lucas was a Couchsurfer who I can contacted because of our mutual interest in UE. We first headed to the Red Hook Grain Elevator, an abandoned grain silo in the Red Hook area -- the apparent appetizer before we would attempt the Williamsburg. "Red Hook" sounds pretty ominous, I remarked. We crossed a wet, dewy soccer field where the water soaked through our socks to our toes, then scaled a brick wall to hop over to the other side, scanning the area, trying to find an in. There were rungs up to the chimney stack of Red Hook but a few were cut off strategically before the 20 ft mark. There were also a few admirable ships at the dock and as we're engrossed in our photography a cat purrs and brushes against us ("Hi kitty! Good kee-tty" Lucas coos). Shortly after a man bikes up to the ship... A middle-aged man who introduced himself as Mattias warned us in a French-like accent "I can tell you guys are pretty, but don't come here without people. theres a guard that comes every 30 min and I could've told security. But I can tell you are pretty so I won't report. Other people come here to do bad things. You are pretty, but it's a bad idea. You should leave right now."  After recapping this encounter with Lucas I realized he was saying "friendly" not "pretty." Oh. It wasn't even midnight yet so the two of us decided to kill time till 2 or 3AM. "That's when there's least people" Lucas mulls. He has never climbed the Williamsburg bridge before either, but we had both watched Undercity, featuring urban explorer Steve Duncan as he climbs the Williamsburg. That was our starting point: that it was possible.
images.alt: Williamsburg Bridge roadway lit up at night, seen from the tower

images.caption: 3:15AM. We approach the bridge and notice there are very few people, mostly drunk couples returning from parties, struggling to ride bikes, struggling to walk. We walk past the first tower "The Manhattan side sees more traffic so let's go to the Brooklyn-side tower" Lucas explains. We stop to put on gloves, jackets, headlamps, and discuss a plan -- not that there was a plan. The tall gate seemed easy to hop, but there was a huge blockage preventing trespassers from immediately accessing the stairs. This meant we would have to climb directly on the bridge lattice like they did in Undercity. Without actually being on the bridge, I found it hard to imagine myself crossing from one side to the other -- dangling feet, a huge drop below to the rush of cars, and an inconveniently placed metal barrier. As we stared at our target silently, we saw a tall man walking up with his bike, approaching us from the distance. He introduced himself with a smile as Paul. I swore he bore a slight resemblance to Steve Duncan himself. Apparently Paul had considered climbing it 3 times before as he biked across but never has … yet. He had spotted us just as he had biked up to the tower on the other side. "I was really annoyed at first. I was waiting for you two to leave so I could try heading up the tower but you weren't leaving. Then I realized what you were up to, of course! And I biked really fast to get all the way here, hoping you'd still be on the walkway when I got here." I was amused. Paul's enthusiasm, despite our cumulative lack of experience, really sparked a determination in our collective group of 3. We swung our legs over the gate and started climbing the metal lattice like cats with our tush in the air, a delicate balancing act. It takes two to tango; three to trespass onto a bridge tower.
images.alt: Bridge deck and Manhattan skyline from the tower top at night

images.caption:
We found a set of rungs in the interior of the bridge and we climbed into a room at the very top of the tower. There were tiny windows with Sharpied graffiti. One read, "The view up here sucks!" 

We walked from one end of the bridge tower to the other and saw a sleeping pad spread out on the floor. I instantly thought back to Moses Gate's book "Hidden Cities" where he described him and his girlfriend having sex on the top of the Williamsburg -- which inspired him to start a Sex on Bridges Club (akin to the Mile High Club.) 

I was standing right there, right now, in the belly of the bridge. At the scene of the crime. There was a window that opened to the cables and Paul and I took turns walking out onto the massive steel cable. It was exhilarating following the curve of the cable down towards the cars below, with a backdrop of a thousand city lights. I would've walked further had I not been afraid of being seen.
images.alt: Suspension cables and steel arches inside the bridge tower
Climber silhouetted in a tower window above the bridge
Manhattan skyline across the East River at night

images.caption:
There must be a way to the very, very top, Paul said. All three of us had watched "Undercity." We should pull it up on our phone and see how they did it, Lucas joked. 

We eventually found a window and opened with some coaxing. The view was stunning; this was only my second time seeing the Manhattan skyline, and was no better place than from the top of this bridge tower, right next to the gigantic red airplane beacon at the apex.
images.alt: Rooftop of the bridge tower overlooking the city lights
